strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: feed-forward zero-shot 3D style transfer from unposed single/multi-view inputs with a reference style image.
The architecture design is reasonable: it builds on strong VGGT/AnySplat-style geometry backbones and separates geometry prediction from style-conditioned color prediction.
The proposed global cross-attention style aggregation is intuitive and ablations compare frame-level, global-level, and hybrid coupling strategies.
The paper evaluates on CO3D, DL3DV-10K, Tanks and Temples, and WikiArt, including cross-category and cross-scene settings.
Qualitative results show plausible stylization and competitive consistency/ArtScore numbers against StyleRF and StyleGS in several scenes.
A reproducibility statement and pseudo-code for style losses are provided, and all datasets used are public.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method largely combines existing VGGT/AnySplat geometry backbones with AdaIN-style cross-attention and statistics matching, without a fundamentally new representation or training paradigm.

The central voxel-based 3D style loss is technically inconsistent: the main text claims multi-view features are fused into a voxel grid before computing statistics, but Algorithm 3 voxelizes each view independently and computes per-view statistics, not scene-level aggregated statistics.

The empirical gains of the proposed 3D style loss are marginal (e.g., Table 2: short-range LPIPS 0.046 vs. 0.046, long-range 0.140 vs. 0.147), with no error bars or significance testing to show they are meaningful.

Evaluation is insufficient for style transfer: there is no quantitative style fidelity/alignment metric, no user study, and no content-preservation metric for stylized outputs; LPIPS/RMSE consistency and ArtScore do not directly validate style transfer quality.
Baselines are limited: only StyleRF and StyleGS are compared, while Styl3R is not compared due to unavailable code; simple per-frame AdaIN or image-to-3DGS style-transfer baselines are also missing.
Important tables are incomplete or poorly formatted (e.g., StyleRF missing Garden in Table 3; malformed header with 'Train' instead of 'Truck'), making comparisons harder to interpret.

The paper overclaims scalability: it states scaling from a single view to hundreds, but Section 4.1 reports quality degradation beyond 32 views and training with no more than 24 views; single-view results also fail to synthesize scene parts.

The claim that global cross-attention benefits geometric detail preservation is unsupported because geometry parameters are predicted from a separate geometry pathway and are not conditioned on the style branch.

Reproducibility is weak: code is not released, and key training details such as loss weights, learning rates, dataset splits, architecture hyperparameters, rendering resolution, and compute are missing; pseudo-code contains ambiguities and likely errors.
There are numerous citation/reference errors and year mismatches that reduce manuscript quality and make positioning harder to assess.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: feed-forward, single-forward multi-view 3D stylization from unposed inputs, without per-scene optimization, which is practically appealing.
The proposed architecture sensibly builds on strong geometry priors from VGGT/AnySplat and injects style through cross-attention rather than modifying the geometry pathway.
The voxel-based 3D style loss is a reasonable extension of AdaIN-style statistics matching into voxel space, and is conceptually aligned with the goal of cross-view consistency.
The paper evaluates on multiple datasets (CO3D, DL3DV-10K, Tanks and Temples) and includes some ablations on attention coupling and style-loss variants.
Qualitative results show stylized renderings that appear to preserve scene structure in several examples, and the appendix provides pseudo-code for the loss functions.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and incremental: the geometry backbone is effectively unchanged VGGT, the style aggregator is mainly global cross-attention with style tokens, and the 3D style loss is largely AdaIN channel-statistics matching applied after voxelization. The core technical contribution is therefore relatively modest for a top-tier venue.

Evaluation of stylization quality is weak. Geometry metrics use the original first frame as the style input, which measures reconstruction rather than style transfer. Cross-view LPIPS/RMSE can be improved by blurring or reducing stylization, and the paper does not report strong style-fidelity metrics such as user studies, FID/KID, CLIP style similarity, or style-loss accuracy against held-out styles.

The reported gains are marginal and may not be statistically meaningful. For example, Table 2 shows short-range LPIPS 0.046 vs 0.046 for image-level and 3D losses, and long-range LPIPS 0.147 vs 0.140; no error bars or significance tests are provided.

Baselines are not fully comparable or complete. The method compares mainly against per-scene StyleRF/StyleGS, while the concurrent single-forward Styl3R is not compared because code is unavailable. This omits the most relevant baseline for the claimed setting.

The ablation in Table 1 has inconsistencies: the text claims the hybrid variant gives an observable donut improvement to 21.4 dB, but the global-only variant reports 22.09 dB. The actual differences between coupling strategies are small, weakening the claimed architectural benefit.

The claim that global cross-attention helps preserve geometry is not well supported: geometry branches are frozen in stage 2 and are not conditioned on style, so geometry predictions should be unaffected by style coupling. The PSNR/SSIM differences likely reflect color/appearance rather than geometric preservation.

Scalability claims are overstated. The abstract says scaling to hundreds of views, but experiments train with no more than 24 views and show quality degradation beyond 32 views, with artifacts at 64 views.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The paper says code will be released but provides no implementation details for training: loss weights, optimizer, learning rate, batch sizes, training schedule, hardware, number of attention blocks, patch encoder details, and voxelization hyperparameters are largely missing.

Method details are incomplete. The differentiable unprojection and voxelization are central to the 3D style loss but are only briefly described. It is unclear how confidence, valid masks, depth, and pose predictions are handled during voxel feature accumulation.

Clarity and referencing issues exist. There are citation-year mismatches (e.g., StyleRF listed as 2024/2023; Galerne et al. 2016 vs 2025), table ambiguities around Train/Garden columns, and minor typographical errors. These reduce confidence in the paper’s rigor.
No limitations or ethical discussion is provided, despite style transfer work raising potential copyright, artist-attribution, and misuse concerns.

strengths: Addresses a challenging and relevant problem: single-forward 3D stylization from unposed multi-view content with only a reference style image, removing the need for per-scene optimization and precomputed camera poses.

The architecture is clearly motivated: geometry predictions remain on the self-attention backbone path while style is injected through global cross-attention, allowing a reasonable disentanglement of geometry and appearance.

The proposed voxel-based 3D style loss extends standard 2D statistics matching into a geometry-aligned 3D space, and the ablation against image-level and scene-level losses shows improved short- and long-range consistency.
The paper evaluates on multiple datasets (CO3D, DL3DV-10K, Tanks and Temples) and reports zero-shot generalization, scaling behavior, and comparisons against StyleRF and StyleGS.
Qualitative results and the global-only cross-attention ablation suggest the method can produce view-consistent stylizations while preserving scene structure.
weaknesses: The evaluation of stylization quality is limited: the main quantitative stylization metrics are consistency and ArtScore, with no direct quantitative measure of style fidelity or content preservation after stylization, and no user study.

Baseline comparisons are narrow. The paper compares mainly against per-scene optimized StyleRF and StyleGS, while the concurrent feed-forward Styl3R is not compared due to unavailable code. The fairness and significance of outperforming per-scene methods in a zero-shot setting are not fully established.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a top-tier venue: no code is provided, and key training details such as hyperparameters, loss weights, model dimensions, dataset splits, optimization settings, and voxelization details are missing or only partially described.

Several tables and claims are inconsistent or incomplete: Table 3/4 appear to omit the Lighthouse scene despite the text referring to four Tanks and Temples scenes, Table 3 has an unexplained empty Train column, and Table 1 is difficult to parse.

The technical novelty is incremental: the method heavily builds on VGGT/AnySplat, and the cross-attention style injection and AdaIN-style statistics matching are well-established. The main novel component, the voxel 3D style loss, is not described in enough implementation detail.

Claims about scaling from one to hundreds of views are only partly supported. The paper qualitatively notes quality degradation beyond 32 views, but provides no quantitative evaluation of stylization quality as the number of views increases.
Ethical and copyright concerns around transferring artistic styles from reference images, especially with WikiArt data, are not discussed.

strengths: Presents a clear and well-motivated framework for single-forward 3D stylization from unposed multi-view inputs, removing per-scene optimization and precomputed poses.

Architecture cleanly separates geometry and style: the geometry path retains self-attention via a VGGT backbone while style is injected through global cross-attention, with prediction heads and a Gaussian adapter that are sensible.
Introduces a voxel-based 3D style loss that extends AdaIN-style feature-statistics matching to voxelized multi-view scene features.
Extensive evaluation across CO3D, DL3DV-10K, and Tanks & Temples, with multiple recent baselines, ablations for coupling strategies and style losses, efficiency analysis, and qualitative results.
Reproducibility is generally strong: implementation details, pseudo-code, loss weights, dataset information, and a code release plan are provided.
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental; the method relies heavily on pretrained VGGT/AnySplat components and the proposed voxel style loss is a fairly straightforward extension of feature-statistics matching.

The central claim that the 3D style loss improves cross-view consistency is not convincingly supported quantitatively: Table 2 shows only marginal differences in short-range and long-range LPIPS/RMSE compared with image- and scene-level losses.

Artistic quality evaluation is limited in scale, using only four Tanks & Temples scenes for comparison and a few CO3D categories for ablations; no user study or large-scale perceptual evaluation is provided.

Comparison fairness is somewhat unclear: per-scene optimization baselines are compared to a feedforward method, StylizedGS is excluded from the main quantitative tables, and differing input resolutions complicate time and quality comparisons.
Ablations do not explore sensitivity to important design choices such as voxel size, loss weighting, style token extraction, or the number/type of style layers.
No discussion of ethical or copyright concerns for style transfer from artistic datasets such as WikiArt and DELAUNAY, which is relevant for this application area.
Minor presentation issues remain, including an apparent typo in Eq. 3 (R_{b,s} instead of R_{b,v}), some table formatting inconsistencies, and an omitted URL for the promised code release.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: feed-forward multi-view 3D stylization from unposed inputs with zero-shot generalization, removing per-scene optimization.
Builds on a strong VGGT/AnySplat-style geometry backbone and proposes a reasonable cross-attention style aggregator to inject style while freezing geometry.
The voxel-based 3D style loss is a plausible extension of AdaIN-style statistics to multi-view voxel features for cross-view consistency.
Includes experiments on CO3D, DL3DV-10K, and Tanks & Temples, with several baselines, ablations, qualitative results, and failure-case analysis.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction/Gaussian splatting components (VGGT, AnySplat, DINO) with a cross-attention style branch and a voxel AdaIN loss; single-forward 3D stylization is already explored by Styl3R.

The main technical contribution, global cross-attention style injection, is not deeply analyzed; the cross-attention ablation evaluates only reconstruction with the first frame as style, not actual stylization quality, so it does not establish that this design improves style transfer.

The voxel-based 3D style loss is under-specified and weakly supported. Algorithm 1 is incomplete, Eq. 5 aligns only global per-channel mean/std between voxelized content features and 2D style features, and the ablation shows scene-level vs. 3D-level differences are negligible (e.g., LPIPS 0.047 vs. 0.047; long-range 0.156 vs. 0.153; ArtScore 9.12 vs. 9.15). This does not convincingly demonstrate a meaningful 3D benefit.

Evaluation of geometry preservation under stylization is missing. Geometry is only tested in a style-free setting and is inherited from frozen VGGT/AnySplat; no pose/depth/reconstruction metrics compare against those backbones, and there is no content-preservation metric for stylized outputs.

Stylization evaluation is insufficient: no user study, no standard style/content loss metrics, no style-fidelity benchmark beyond ArtScore/ArtFID, and no statistical significance tests. Consistency metrics can be gamed by over-smoothed outputs.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair or complete. Stylos is trained once on large-scale data and compared to per-scene/per-style optimization baselines whose training time is included; Styl3R results are missing for the Truck scene; StylizedGS is excluded from main quantitative comparisons due to 'failures' but included in appendix, raising cherry-picking concerns. Resolutions and protocols also differ.

Scalability and real-time claims are overstated. The paper admits quality degrades beyond 32 views, and appendix shows 64 views take 4.83s per batch with linear memory growth; the headline 0.05s latency is for a restricted setting/resolution.

Reproducibility is inconsistent: the abstract/contributions say code is available, but no URL is given, and the reproducibility statement says implementation will be released only upon acceptance. Several details (voxelization gradients, style-token construction, exact style loss normalization) are missing.

Clarity and presentation suffer from incomplete equations/algorithm (Eq. 3 contains undefined R_{b,s}; Algorithm 1 line 9 is incomplete), confusing table formatting, typos, and occasional overstated language.
Ethical/legal considerations around artistic style imitation and use of copyrighted artworks are not discussed.

strengths: Well-motivated single-forward framework for unposed multi-view 3D stylization, combining feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction with reference-style conditioning and avoiding per-scene optimization or precomputed poses.

Introduces a style aggregator with global cross-attention between content and style tokens, and systematically compares frame, global, and hybrid coupling strategies, showing that global-only coupling better preserves geometry in the studied setting.

Proposes a voxel-based 3D style loss that aggregates multi-view VGG features into a voxel grid and aligns their statistics with style statistics, improving cross-view consistency and geometry-aware stylization.

Extensive experiments across CO3D, DL3DV-10K, and Tanks & Temples with unseen styles and zero-shot generalization; compares against recent 3D stylization baselines and reports consistency, artistic quality, and speed.
Includes ablation studies on coupling strategies and style losses, qualitative comparisons, failure-case analysis, efficiency scaling, and reproducibility details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method builds heavily on VGGT/AnySplat, cross-attention style injection, and AdaIN-style statistics extended to voxel space, rather than introducing a fundamentally new formulation.

Scalability claims are overstrong: the abstract and introduction advertise scaling to hundreds of views, but experiments show degraded quality beyond 32 views and failures at very small view counts; limitations later acknowledge VGGT backbone instability.

Evaluation raises fairness concerns: excluding StylizedGS failure cases from consistency and ArtScore comparisons may bias results, and comparisons mix per-scene optimization methods with single-forward methods; no human study is provided for stylization quality.

Ablations are somewhat limited: the style-loss ablation uses only 15 CO3D scenes with small consistency differences and no variance estimates, while the cross-attention ablation covers only three categories; no ablation on voxel size, loss weights, or training view counts.

Some technical/writing slips are present, e.g., the standard-deviation term in Eq. 3 appears to use the wrong index, Algorithm 1 line 9 is incomplete, and full code is only promised rather than released.

The 3D style loss matches global mean/std statistics, which may ignore spatial layout and local style patterns; handling of empty voxels, scale sensitivity, and voxelization choices are not analyzed in depth.
